title: Travel Columns
description: Ten warm, reflective travel columns by different writers: a slow train through the Rockies, a market in Oaxaca, a rainy week in Edinburgh, Route 66, a Greek ferry, a Kyoto inn, the Maine coast, a desert camp in Morocco, and two columns about the craft and the cost of travel.

lessons.title: The Slow Train West of Jasper
lessons.summary: A writer rides a slow train through the Canadian Rockies, past glaciers and limestone cliffs, beside a young family and their baby.
lessons.text:
Some trains are built to save time. The one I boarded in Jasper, in the Canadian Rockies, seemed built to spend it, and I was happy to let it.

I had a seat in the dome car, a carriage with a glass roof, so that nothing stood between me and the mountains. Across the aisle sat a young couple with a baby of about eight months and a stuffed panda that the baby refused to let go of. The panda, black and white and a little gray from being loved, traveled the whole way on her lap.

West of Jasper, the train settled into the tempo of a long walk. Its wheels rattled over the joints in the rails with a steady rhythm, and after an hour the rattle had become as calming as rain on a roof. The baby fell asleep to it, and her father whispered that a rattle like this worked better than any song.

Then the first great vista opened. Mount Robson, the highest peak in the Canadian Rockies, rose above the valley with snow on its shoulders, and high on its slopes lay a glacier, blue and white, that looked perfectly still. I had always pictured a glacier as a frozen lake, but a glacier is really a river of ice that moves a little every year. A man behind me, who had once worked as a park guide, told us that the thickness of the ice in the great fields of ice south of Jasper reaches about 1,000 feet in places. That thickness was shrinking, he added softly, and the glacier he had known as a young man had moved back up the mountain.

He also explained the rock. Much of the Canadian Rockies is limestone, formed from the shells of tiny sea creatures that lived in an ancient ocean. I looked at the gray limestone cliffs and tried to imagine fish swimming where the snow now lay.

As we went down, the vegetation changed. Near the high passes there was little but moss and low bushes. Lower down, dark pine forests closed in around the tracks, and by evening, as we followed a river, the vegetation had become soft and green, with yellow leaves among the pines.

At one point the baby woke up crying, and her mother changed her diaper on a narrow seat with the speed of long practice. A crying baby, a clean diaper, a sleeping child again: on a train that moved at the tempo of ordinary life, it seemed the most natural thing in the world.

When the light faded, the vista outside turned blue, then black. The baby sighed softly in her sleep, and as I listened to the rattle of the wheels, I thought that a slow train is one of the last places where time still belongs to you.

Questions:
Why did the writer choose a seat in the dome car?
The dome car had a glass roof, so nothing stood between the writer and the mountains.
What did the baby hold for the whole trip?
She held a stuffed panda, which traveled the whole way on her lap.
What is a glacier, according to the column?
A glacier is a river of ice that moves a little every year.
What is much of the Canadian Rockies made of?
Much of it is limestone, formed from the shells of tiny sea creatures in an ancient ocean.

lessons.title: A Market Morning in Oaxaca
lessons.summary: A writer spends a morning in a market in Oaxaca with a chocolate seller who teaches her about food, words and the city.
lessons.text:
The first thing anyone in Oaxaca will teach you is how to pronounce the name of the city. It is wah-HAH-kah, and the women in the market corrected me patiently until I could pronounce it without thinking.

I arrived at the market at seven, while the sellers were still setting out their goods. Oaxaca lies in a high valley in southern Mexico, and the morning air was cool and smelled of wood smoke and coffee. Inside the long, roofed hall, the food was so abundant that I had to stop and simply look. There were piles of tomatoes and limes, chilies of every shape and color, and bunches of herbs I could not name. Fruit was just as abundant: mangoes, pineapples and bananas. Near the door, a boy cut long green stalks of sugarcane into short pieces for children to chew. One small girl held a stalk in each hand and chewed on each in turn.

My guide that morning was Lucía, who had sold chocolate in the market for twenty-five years. Her stand smelled delightful, of cinnamon and roasted cocoa. She ground cocoa beans with sugar and cinnamon and pressed the paste into round tablets, which people melt into hot water or milk. With the chocolate she sold a soft egg bread with a shiny golden crust. "You dip the bread in the chocolate until the crust is soft," she told me, "but not so long that it falls in." I failed twice before I learned the timing, and the result was delightful.

Lucía also taught me a word. In English, a mole is a small animal that digs under the ground, but in Mexico the noun means a thick, dark sauce made with chilies, seeds, spices and sometimes chocolate. The noun comes from an old Nahuatl word for sauce. Oaxaca is famous for its moles.

Behind her stand hung a bright poster for a wrestling night. It showed a wrestler in a silver mask with his arms raised. Mexican wrestling is a family event, she explained, and every masked wrestler plays either a hero or a villain, whom the crowd cheers or loves to boo. Her grandson wanted to be a wrestler when he grew up.

When I paid, she did not use a machine. She wrote each price on a scrap of paper, kept a quick tally in her head and then showed me the tally so that I could check it. It was correct to the last coin.

Before I left, she told me to visit the great church of the Virgin of Solitude, the patron saint of the city. Inside, I found candles and flowers left by families from the villages, a quiet devotion that has lasted for centuries. Later I recognized the same devotion in the way Lucía arranged her chocolate each morning: carefully, as if it mattered, because to her it did.

Questions:
How do you pronounce the name of the city?
You pronounce it wah-HAH-kah, with the stress in the middle.
How do you eat the egg bread with the chocolate?
You dip the bread in the chocolate until the crust is soft, but not so long that it falls in.
What does the noun mole mean in Mexico?
It means a thick, dark sauce made with chilies, seeds, spices and sometimes chocolate.
How did Lucía keep a tally of the prices?
She wrote each price on paper and showed the writer the tally.

lessons.title: Seven Wet Days in Edinburgh
lessons.summary: A writer spends a rainy week in Edinburgh, climbing a hill, visiting a bookshop and talking with a retired minister.
lessons.text:
It rained for seven days in Edinburgh, and I would not change a single one of them.

People warn you about the weather in Scotland as if it were a flaw. I had packed a small folding umbrella, which proved insufficient on the first afternoon, when the wind came up from the sea and turned it inside out. A woman at a bus stop told me kindly that an umbrella was insufficient protection here and that I needed a good coat with a hood. The next morning I bought one. Its hood had a small flap that closed over the neck, and on windy days the flap beat against my collar like the wing of a bird.

On the second day I climbed Arthur's Seat, an old volcano that rises right beside the city. Its slopes are rough heath, open land covered in grass and low, tough plants. The path across the heath was muddy, and the turf on either side was as wet as a sponge. A local runner passed me with a long, easy stride, as if the steep turf were a flat street. I tried to copy her stride and failed. At the brow of the hill, just below the top, the rain thinned, and the whole city appeared below me: the castle on its rock, the gray roofs, the sea beyond. I stood at the brow for a long time, cold and very happy.

On a curving street of painted shop fronts in the old town, I found a shop that sold old books. Its owner showed me a folio of prints of the city. A folio, he explained, is a large book made from sheets folded only once, so its pages are big enough for wide pictures.

He also told me about a darker page of the city's past. In the early nineteenth century, Edinburgh's medical schools needed bodies for their students to study, and there were never enough. Some men dug up the newly buried at night and sold them to the schools. People called them resurrection men, a grim reference to the Christian belief in the resurrection of the dead. At Greyfriars churchyard, I later saw the iron cages that families once placed over graves to protect them.

At Greyfriars I met an elderly man in a raincoat who turned out to be a retired reverend. The reverend told me that he had trained as a minister at New College, the university's school of divinity, which stands on a hill above the city's gardens. Students still come there for theological study, he said. We talked about theological questions and about the weather in roughly equal measure. When I asked whether the rain ever bothered him, the reverend smiled. "It keeps the city green," he said, "and it keeps the visitors humble."

Questions:
Why did the writer buy a coat with a hood?
The umbrella proved insufficient, because the wind turned it inside out.
What is the land on the slopes of Arthur's Seat like?
It is rough heath, open land with grass and low, tough plants, and the turf was very wet.
What is a folio?
A folio is a large book made from sheets folded only once, with pages big enough for wide pictures.
Why were some men called resurrection men?
They dug up the newly buried and sold the bodies to medical schools, as if they raised the dead.

lessons.title: Route 66 in My Father's Car
lessons.summary: A writer drives part of Route 66 in her father's forty-year-old car and meets a motel owner whose family kept going when the highway was bypassed.
lessons.text:
My father bought his car new when he was twenty-five, and he drove it for forty years. When he finally stopped driving, he gave me the keys and one piece of advice: "Take her west on Route 66, and don't go faster than she wants to go."

Route 66 opened in 1926 and ran about 2,400 miles from Chicago to Santa Monica, on the coast of California. During the hard years of the Great Depression, families from the farm states traveled it west in search of work, and the novelist John Steinbeck dubbed it "the Mother Road." The name stayed. Road fans also like to dub it the Main Street of America, a nickname from its early years.

The car was remarkably simple. The gear lever was on the steering column, not between the seats, and it took me a whole day to learn to move the lever without looking. The wheels were plain steel, heavier than the light alloy wheels of modern cars. An alloy is a metal made by mixing two or more metals, and the mechanic who checked the car in Chicago said, with some respect, that nothing on it was made of alloy except the radio.

What I had not expected was the amusement. Route 66 was built for people who drove slowly and needed reasons to stop, and its business owners competed to be noticed. In Oklahoma I saw a giant blue whale built beside a pond. In Texas, near Amarillo, I walked out to a field where ten old cars stand nose-down in the ground, covered in paint by visitors. Each hulk is a different color every year, because people bring spray cans and add their own. It was outrageous, and it was meant to be outrageous. A child next to me laughed with pure amusement and painted a small yellow heart on the nearest hulk.

The road also had a sadder story. In later decades, the new interstate highways bypassed one town after another, and drivers no longer passed by. Many motels, diners and gas stations went bankrupt. In New Mexico, I spent a night at a small motel run by a woman named Irene. Her parents bought it in 1955, she told me, and when the interstate opened, they nearly went bankrupt too. They owed money to the bank, and their creditor wanted to sell the property. Her father drove to the city, sat in the creditor's office and asked for one more year. He got it.

The family decided to rename the motel to attract new guests. They had called it simply the Western Motel, but they chose to rename it the Desert Rose, after the flowers her mother grew by the door. Remarkably, the new name, a fresh coat of paint and a new sign brought the guests back.

I drove on to the Pacific, never faster than the car wanted to go.

Questions:
What did John Steinbeck dub Route 66?
He dubbed it "the Mother Road."
Where was the gear lever in the old car?
It was on the steering column, not between the seats.
What is an alloy?
An alloy is a metal made by mixing two or more metals.
What happened to many businesses when the interstates bypassed their towns?
Many motels, diners and gas stations went bankrupt.
How did Irene's father deal with the family's creditor?
He sat in the creditor's office and asked for one more year, and he got it.

lessons.title: A Ferry to Amorgos
lessons.summary: A writer waits for a delayed ferry from Athens, sails through the Greek islands and climbs to a monastery built into a cliff.
lessons.text:
The ferry to Amorgos was supposed to leave the port of Piraeus, near Athens, at seven in the morning. I had bought my ticket through a small travel agency, which gave me a voucher instead of a ticket. At the port, I joined a line of travelers waiting to exchange a voucher for a real ticket at a window. A strong summer wind from the north was blowing, and the ferry left two hours late.

Nobody seemed upset by the inconvenience. An old man next to me shrugged and said that in the islands the wind decides, not the timetable. By the time we sailed, the inconvenience had become a small, pleasant memory.

I watched the loading from the upper deck. The back of the ship opened slowly, and a wide ramp came down on hydraulic arms, moving with a soft, steady hum. Trucks carrying water, food and building materials drove into the ship, followed by cars. When the ramp rose again, the hydraulic arms locked it into place, and we were off.

The ferry stopped at four islands before mine. At each one, the same scene played out: the ship backed toward a small white town, the ramp came down, and people on the dock waved to relatives on board. At one port the sea was rough, and when the captain finally brought the ship safely against the dock, several passengers began to applaud. I did not know whether to applaud too, but everyone around me did, so I joined in.

We reached Amorgos in the afternoon. The crowd on the dock began to disperse at once, some into waiting cars, some on foot up the hill, and within ten minutes the crowd had dispersed and the dock was empty. I liked the island's mentality immediately. Shops opened when their owners arrived, and lunch lasted as long as the conversation did. It is a mentality, I think, that comes from living by the sea and the wind.

The next morning, I climbed to the monastery of Hozoviotissa. The monastery was built more than nine hundred years ago, and it hangs on a cliff high above the sea, white against the brown rock. On the beach below, people lay in the sun in bikinis, but visitors to the monastery are obliged to dress modestly, with their shoulders and knees covered. Women in a bikini or shorts are given a long skirt at the door. The monks still feel obliged to welcome every visitor, and a monk offered me cold water and a small sweet.

On my last evening, I allowed myself to indulge. I ate grilled fish, a salad of tomatoes and local cheese, and a honey cake that the owner of the café insisted I try. "On Amorgos," she said, "you indulge a little, or you don't really visit."

Questions:
What did the writer need to exchange at the port?
The writer needed to exchange a voucher for a real ticket.
Why did the ferry leave two hours late?
A strong summer wind from the north was blowing.
How did the ramp at the back of the ship move?
It came down and rose again on hydraulic arms.
Why did several passengers applaud at one port?
They applauded because the captain brought the ship safely against the dock in a rough sea.
What are visitors to the monastery obliged to do?
They are obliged to dress modestly, with their shoulders and knees covered.

lessons.title: Three Nights in a Kyoto Inn
lessons.summary: A writer stays at a small traditional inn in Kyoto and learns from its owner about rooms, gardens and quiet.
lessons.text:
The inn where I stayed in Kyoto had only six rooms, and on my first evening I understood that its simplicity was not an accident but a choice.

My room had a floor of tatami, the woven straw mats found in traditional Japanese houses, a low table, two cushions and a sliding paper door that opened onto a tiny garden. There was nothing else. The owner, Mrs. Mori, explained that Japanese rooms are measured in mats, so that a room is described as a six-mat or eight-mat room. It is a spatial language, she said, in which you understand the size of a room by counting the mats under your feet. After a day, my own spatial sense changed, and I was counting mats too.

Mrs. Mori offered an analogy that I have thought about ever since. An empty room, she said, is like a stage before a play begins: it is not empty of meaning, only waiting. I liked the analogy very much.

At dinner, I sat on my knees in the traditional way, with my back straight. Mrs. Mori kept a perfect posture for an hour while she served the small dishes one by one. My own posture lasted about ten minutes before my legs went numb. She noticed, smiled and quietly brought me a low chair.

I made a more embarrassing mistake with the cotton robe the inn provides. I had wrapped it with the right side over the left. Mrs. Mori softly corrected it, explaining that the left side always goes over the right, because the opposite way is used only to dress the dead. I felt myself blush.

The garden outside my door was only a few steps wide, but Mrs. Mori's grandfather had taken a whole year to compose it, as a painter might compose a picture. Moss covered the ground between three dark stones. Mrs. Mori told me that moss needs the right substrate, a layer of soil and fine stone that holds water without becoming mud. Strong sun, she added, would inhibit the moss, so a maple tree had been planted to shade it. Around the moss lay white gravel, raked into lines as sharp as a razor. Each morning a gardener raked them again, so straight that they looked drawn with a razor.

I had brought a notebook and meant to compose a short poem about the garden. I never finished it. The quiet of the inn seemed to inhibit words rather than invite them, and I came to feel that this was the point. Fundamentally, a place like this does not sell comfort or luxury. Fundamentally, it sells simplicity and attention.

Questions:
How are Japanese rooms measured?
They are measured in mats, so a room is described as a six-mat or eight-mat room.
What analogy did Mrs. Mori offer about an empty room?
She said an empty room is like a stage before a play begins.
Why did the writer blush?
The writer had wrapped the robe with the right side over the left, which is the wrong way.
What does moss need, according to Mrs. Mori?
It needs the right substrate, a layer of soil and fine stone that holds water without becoming mud.
Why did the writer never finish the poem?
The quiet of the inn seemed to inhibit words rather than invite them.

lessons.title: Autumn on the Maine Coast
lessons.summary: A writer takes his elderly father, who has dementia, back to the coast where the father spent his childhood summers.
lessons.text:
Every autumn, visitors come to Maine to see the trees change color, and every autumn they rave about it. Friends had raved to me for years about the red maples against the gray sea. This October I finally went, with my father, who is eighty-one and has dementia.

We went to a small fishing village where my father's maternal grandparents, his mother's parents, had lived. He had spent every summer there as a boy. The doctors had told us that dementia often takes the recent past first and leaves the distant past for longer, and so it was. My father could not remember what he had eaten for breakfast, but in the village he could recount, in perfect detail, the summers of his childhood.

He would recount the same stories several times a day. His maternal grandfather had fished for lobster from a small wooden boat, leaving the harbor before dawn. His grandmother had baked bread every morning in a black iron stove. I had heard these stories before, but hearing them by the water, in the very place they happened, made them new.

Walking was hard for my father until the spring, when a steroid injection in his knee eased the pain. Without the steroid, he told me, he would have stayed in the car. Instead, he walked with me every day along the rocky shore, holding my arm.

I had brought my camera and a macro lens, which lets you photograph very small things from very close. While my father sat on a rock, I took macro pictures of the tide pools: tiny snails, pink weeds, the bright orange of a sea star. In one picture, the lines on a shell looked exactly like a fingerprint. When I showed him, my father pressed his own thumb next to the screen and laughed, leaving a fingerprint on the glass. "Every shell is different," he said. "Like people."

There is a particular cruelty in dementia, and I felt it more than once that week. One evening my father asked me, politely, whether I had children of my own, as if he were meeting me for the first time. The cruelty is not that the person disappears, but that he is still there, still kind, still himself, and yet he cannot always find you.

But I also learned that the illness does not take everything at once. On our last morning, the trees above the harbor were red and gold, and the sea was a calm, cold blue. My father stood at the edge of the dock, looked at the boats and said, "My grandfather would have gone out today." He was right. It was a perfect day for fishing, and for remembering.

Questions:
What do visitors to Maine rave about in autumn?
They rave about the changing colors, especially the red maples against the gray sea.
Who were the father's maternal grandparents?
They were his mother's parents, who had lived in the fishing village.
What could the father recount in perfect detail?
He could recount the summers of his childhood in the village.
What does a macro lens let you do?
It lets you photograph very small things from very close.
What, according to the writer, is the cruelty of dementia?
The person is still there and still kind, but he cannot always find you.

lessons.title: A Night Among the Dunes
lessons.summary: A writer spends a night at a desert camp in Morocco with a local guide and a science teacher from the United Arab Emirates.
lessons.text:
The road ends at Merzouga, a small town on the edge of the Sahara in southeastern Morocco. Beyond it lie the great dunes of Erg Chebbi, hills of orange sand that rise as high as a tall building. I reached the camp the way many visitors do: by jeep for the first part, then on a camel for the last hour, as the sun went down.

My guide was Youssef, an Amazigh man whose family has lived on the edge of the desert for generations. Twice a week, he told me, the jeep brings supplies to the camp, and the camp keeps a cache of water and firewood behind the largest tent. Without that cache, no one could stay more than a night.

There were only six guests that evening. One of them was Mariam, a science teacher from Abu Dhabi. She explained to the rest of us that Abu Dhabi is both a city and an emirate, one of the seven emirates that together form the United Arab Emirates.

Dinner was a tagine, a stew cooked slowly in a clay pot with a tall cone-shaped lid. Ours held a lamb shank cooked for hours with dried fruit, almonds and spices until the meat fell from the bone. Youssef's mother, he said, makes lamb shank the same way for celebrations.

After dinner, we walked away from the tents and lay on the cold sand. The moon had not yet risen, and the stars were thicker than I had ever seen them. Youssef explained that his family still follows the lunar calendar for religious holidays. Because the lunar year is about eleven days shorter than the solar year, he said, the holy month of Ramadan arrives a little earlier every year.

Then a bright line of light crossed the sky, and someone asked whether it was a comet. Mariam said no, it was a meteor, a grain of dust burning up in the air. A comet is a ball of ice and dust far away in space, and it can hang in the sky for weeks with its long tail.

I asked Youssef whether he carried a compass in the desert. He laughed and said he had never needed a compass. He reads the shapes of the dunes by day and the stars by night. His grandfather, he added, had been the sheikh of their village, the respected elder whom families visited when they could not agree about land or water. The old sheikh taught him the stars when he was six.

When the moon finally rose, the dunes turned silver, and the whole desert looked lunar, like the surface of another world. I stayed outside until I was too cold to stay any longer.

Questions:
How did the writer reach the camp?
The writer went by jeep for the first part and then on a camel for the last hour.
What is Abu Dhabi, according to Mariam?
It is both a city and an emirate, one of the seven emirates of the United Arab Emirates.
What is the difference between a comet and a meteor?
A meteor is a grain of dust burning up in the air, while a comet is a ball of ice and dust far away in space.
Why did Youssef not need a compass?
He reads the shapes of the dunes by day and the stars by night.

lessons.title: How This Column Gets Written
lessons.summary: A travel columnist explains the rules she follows: she pays her own way, travels without announcing herself and writes and rewrites with care.
lessons.text:
Readers sometimes ask me how this column is made, so this week, instead of a place, I would like to describe the work itself.

I learned the job during an internship at a city newspaper, the summer I turned twenty-two. My internship was mostly answering phones and checking facts, but the travel editor, a patient man near retirement, taught me two things I still believe. The first was fairness. "Every place deserves fairness," he said, "including the ones you didn't enjoy." Fairness means describing a rainy town as it is, and also as it might be on a sunny day.

The second thing he taught me was to pay my own way. Many hotels, airlines and tourist boards offer writers free trips, and some columns depend on that kind of sponsorship. I understand why: travel is expensive, and newspapers have little money. But a column paid for by sponsorship is harder to trust. If a hotel has given you a free room, how credible is your praise of its breakfast? To stay credible, this paper pays for everything I do, and when a business offers me a gift, I refuse. I forfeit a lot of free dinners that way, and I would forfeit many more before I would lose a reader's trust.

For the same reason, I travel undercover. Like any good restaurant reviewer, I book under my own name but never say what I do. A reviewer who announces herself gets the best table, the freshest bread and the warmest smile, and then writes about an experience that nobody else will have. Traveling undercover, I get the room by the elevator, just like you would.

These days, the paper also watches the analytics of every column: how many people open it online, how far they read and where they stop. I was suspicious of analytics at first, but they have taught me something useful. Readers leave when a column loses its story. They stay when there is a person, a place and a reason to keep going.

Then comes the writing, which takes longer than the trip. I write a first draft in a single day and then spend a week trying to tweak it. I tweak a verb, remove an adjective, move a paragraph. My old editor hated the colon. He said a colon was a door that a lazy writer opened instead of building a proper sentence. I still use the colon, but only when a sentence truly needs a pause before the thing it promises.

Finally, I read the column aloud. If I stumble over a sentence, a reader will too. When I can read the whole piece without stopping, I send it in, and I start planning the next trip.

Questions:
Where did the writer learn the job?
She learned it during an internship at a city newspaper.
What did the travel editor mean by fairness?
He meant that every place deserves to be described as it is, including the ones you didn't enjoy.
Why does the writer refuse sponsorship and gifts?
She believes a column paid for by sponsorship is harder to trust, and she wants to stay credible.
Why does the writer travel undercover?
A reviewer who announces herself gets special treatment that nobody else will have.
What has the writer learned from the analytics?
She has learned that readers leave when a column loses its story.

lessons.title: The Case for the Slow Way
lessons.summary: A columnist weighs flying against taking the train and explains why she now travels slowly when she can.
lessons.text:
For most of my working life, I flew everywhere. A column about a city three thousand miles away began with an airport, a plane and a tired arrival. In the last few years, however, I have taken the train whenever I can, and readers often ask me why. The honest answer is less simple than they expect.

The obvious reason is sustainability. Comparative studies of the two ways of traveling are clear: for the same distance, a train usually produces a small fraction of the emissions of a plane. If sustainability means using the world in a way that leaves enough for those who come after us, then the train is, in most cases, the better choice. I think about our offspring, and their offspring, and the kind of planet they will inherit. That is not a small consideration.

But I do not want to pretend that the question is closed. There is no neat theorem that proves the train is always right. A comparative look at prices shows that trains are often more expensive, and they take far longer. A nurse with one week of vacation cannot spend four days of it on a train. A family with three children may not be able to afford it. Any honest theorem about travel would need a long list of exceptions.

Nor is my choice ideological. Some readers, on both sides, want it to be. One man wrote to call me an extremist for suggesting that people fly less; another reader called me a hypocrite for flying at all. I am neither an extremist nor a saint. I still fly to see my sister on the other side of the ocean, and I will keep doing so. My choice is not an ideological position but a practical one, made trip by trip.

I should also admit a small vanity. It is pleasant to feel good about yourself, and there is a vanity in telling others how you travel, which is, after all, what I am doing now. I try to remember that one person's habits matter less than the choices made by governments and companies, and that a column about trains does not save the planet by itself.

Still, there is one reason that has nothing to do with numbers. The train has made me a better traveler. From a window seat, I see the land change slowly, from farms to forests to mountains, and I arrive knowing where I am. A plane delivers you to a place; a train introduces you to it. That, more than any study, is why I keep choosing the slow way.

Questions:
What is the obvious reason the writer gives for taking the train?
The obvious reason is sustainability, because a train usually produces far fewer emissions than a plane.
What do comparative studies show about trains and planes?
They show that, for the same distance, a train produces a small fraction of the emissions of a plane.
Why does the writer say there is no neat theorem about travel?
Trains are often more expensive and slower, so the train is not always the right choice for everyone.
What did one reader call the writer?
He called her an extremist for suggesting that people fly less.
What reason has nothing to do with numbers?
The train has made her a better traveler, because she sees the land change slowly and arrives knowing where she is.
